body.title: Books on a shelf
body.tagline: A teacher's own application, carried through every phase.
body.description: Shelf keeps the books a small library owns: a Python API that adds, lists and lends books, and a React page that shows them in shelf order. You will write a missing story, sketch the contract, implement the marked gaps in both layers, prove the behaviour with tests, package the API, and ship a change request that reorders the shelf.

phases.title: Requirements
phases.intro: Four stories are settled. Write the fifth, the one a member asked for, with criteria a tester could check.

tasks.title: Requirements
tasks.brief:
Requirements: write the missing story

The shelf's backlog has four settled stories. A member has asked for a fifth: to see which of an author's books are free to borrow right now. Write SH-5 in the story form in this room; it is saved as requirements/story.json.

What good looks like

- One story in the As a … I want … so that … form, naming who wants it and why.
- At least two acceptance criteria in the Given … When … Then … form: tag one happy path and one boundary, the book that is already on loan.
- At least one thing the story leaves out of scope.

Using the AI mentor well

Ask the mentor to question your story, not to write it: "what would a tester ask about this criterion?" gets you further than "write SH-5".

criteria.title: Story
criteria.description: Who wants it, what they want, and why.

criteria.title: Acceptance criteria
criteria.description: Given / When / Then criteria a tester could check, including a book on loan.

criteria.title: Completeness
criteria.description: Enough criteria and scope lines to say what is in and what is left out.

objectives: Write SH-5 in the As a / I want / so that form
Give it at least two Given / When / Then acceptance criteria
Cover the case of a book that is already on loan

providedStories.title: Browse the shelf
providedStories.capability: to see every book in shelf order
providedStories.benefit: I can find one without asking

criteria.then: they are listed by title

criteria.when: I filter by an author in any case
criteria.then: only that author's books are listed

providedStories.title: Lend a book
providedStories.capability: to record who has borrowed a book

criteria.when: I lend it to a member
criteria.then: the book says who has it

criteria.when: I try to lend it again
criteria.then: the loan is refused

providedStories.title: Return a book
providedStories.capability: to put a returned book back
providedStories.benefit: the next member can borrow it

criteria.then: it is on the shelf again
the request is refused as not found

providedStories.capability: the shelf to say which books are on loan
providedStories.benefit: I do not walk to an empty space

criteria.then: the line ends "on loan"

phases.title: Design
phases.intro: Write down what the shelf API answers before anyone builds it: every operation, every refusal, one decision.

tasks.title: Design
tasks.brief:
Design: the shelf's contract

Fill the design in the Design room's forms: the entities and operations on the UML model tab, the endpoints and the error catalogue on the API contract tab, and one decision with its reason.

What good looks like

- The errors: which status a refusal carries (a book nobody has, a book already on loan) and the error code in its body.
- One decision, the alternative you rejected, and the reason, in a sentence with because in it.

criteria.title: Contract
criteria.description: Every operation the stories need, and every refusal with its status and error code, as a client would need them.

criteria.title: Decision
criteria.description: A decision, the alternative it beat and the reason.

criteria.title: Completeness
criteria.description: Every story the design lists is served by an operation, and every operation names its inputs and what it returns.

objectives: List every operation the API answers
Name the status and error code of every refusal
Record one decision, the alternative and the reason

stories.title: Browse the shelf
stories.line: As a member, I want to see every book in shelf order, so that I can find one without asking.

stories.title: Lend a book
stories.line: As a librarian, I want to record who has borrowed a book, so that I know where it is.

stories.title: Return a book
stories.line: As a librarian, I want to put a returned book back, so that the next member can borrow it.

phases.title: Implementation
phases.intro: The shelf runs except for four marked gaps, two in the Python API and two in the TypeScript page. Make the backlog's rules true in both.

tasks.title: Implementation
tasks.brief:
Implementation: fill the marked gaps

The shelf runs except for four marked gaps: two in the Python API (api/shelf.py: books and lend) and two in the TypeScript page (web/src/lib/shelf.ts: shelfLabel and sortForShelf). Make the backlog's rules true in both layers.

What good looks like

- books lists by title ignoring case, then id, and the author filter ignores case and surrounding spaces.
- lend refuses an unknown id, a blank borrower, and a book already on loan.
- shelfLabel and sortForShelf agree with the API about what a person reads.
- The visible tests pass before you submit; the hidden suites ask more.

Using the AI mentor well

Paste the failing test's name, not your whole file, and ask what rule it is checking. The mentor explains; it does not write the function for you.

criteria.description: You ran the tests before submitting and used the mentor in moderation.

Implement lend and its refusals (SH-2)
Implement shelfLabel so a lent book says so (SH-4)
Implement sortForShelf so the page agrees with the API (SH-1)

phases.title: Testing
phases.intro: Write the acceptance suites that prove SH-1 to SH-4 on both sides, and catch the bugs planted in copies of the application.

tasks.title: Testing
tasks.brief:
Testing: prove the backlog

Write acceptance tests for SH-1 to SH-4 in tests/test_acceptance.py (the API) and web/src/lib/acceptance.test.ts (the page). The graders run your suites against the working application and against copies of it with bugs planted in them; a good suite passes on the first and fails on every one of the others.

What good looks like

- Every test passes against the working application.
- At least one test per acceptance criterion, asserting what a person or a client would see, not only a status code.
- Cases about the author filter, lending, returning and the "on loan" line.

Using the AI mentor well

Ask the mentor which acceptance criterion a test of yours does not yet cover.

criteria.description: The author filter, lending, returning and the on-loan line each have a test.

objectives: Turn SH-1, SH-2 and SH-3 into tests over the HTTP contract
Prove the shelf line and the shelf order on the page
Make every test pass against the working application
Write assertions sharp enough to fail on every broken copy

phases.title: Deployment
phases.intro: Finish the API's image definition and the runbook, run the selfcheck, then run the drill and write down what broke.

tasks.title: Deployment
tasks.brief:
Finish api/Dockerfile so the image starts the API, and write the runbook an operator reads at 3am in the Runbook tab. Then run the selfcheck, and run the drill: a broken configuration is swapped in, and you write down what broke.

What good looks like: the Dockerfile sets a working directory, copies the application and starts api/main.py in exec form, with no TODO left. The runbook in the Runbook tab says how to check the service is healthy under Health checks and how to roll back under Rollback; its Environment and Data sections are there for anything else an operator needs. The incident is closed on the drill page with what the drill broke, the fix and one action item.

Using the AI mentor well: ask what each Dockerfile instruction changes about the image, and write the instructions yourself.

criteria.title: Runbook quality
criteria.description: Health check, rollback and the incident, written for someone who was not there.

Write the runbook: health check, rollback, incident

phases.intro: Change request CHG-1 arrives on a shelf that already works: shelve by surname. Ship it in both layers without breaking anything.

tasks.title: Maintenance
tasks.brief:
Change request CHG-1. The library has asked for the shelf to follow the order a librarian shelves in: by the author's surname, then by title, then by id. Change both layers (api/shelf.py and web/src/lib/shelf.ts) without breaking anything the shelf already did.

What good looks like: the API and the page agree on the new order. Lending, returning and the author filter behave exactly as before. The visible regression cases pass before you submit.

Record the change in the change request as you go: in the Request tab, what the change touches; in the Checks tab, the tests and the acceptance items each covers; in the Release tab, the release, its change lines and how to roll it back.

Using the AI mentor well: ask the mentor which existing behaviour your change could break, then run the regression cases to find out.

body.title: Books on a shelf
body.tagline: A teacher's own application, carried through every phase.
body.description: Shelf keeps the books a small library owns: a Python API that adds, lists and lends books, and a React page that shows them in shelf order. You will write a missing story, sketch the contract, implement the marked gaps in both layers, prove the behaviour with tests, package the API, and ship a change request that reorders the shelf.

phases.title: Requirements
phases.intro: Four stories are settled. Write the fifth, the one a member asked for, with criteria a tester could check.

tasks.title: Requirements
tasks.brief:
Requirements: write the missing story

The shelf's backlog has four settled stories. A member has asked for a fifth: to see which of an author's books are free to borrow right now. Write SH-5 in the story form in this room; it is saved as requirements/story.json.

What good looks like

- One story in the As a … I want … so that … form, naming who wants it and why.
- At least two acceptance criteria in the Given … When … Then … form: tag one happy path and one boundary, the book that is already on loan.
- At least one thing the story leaves out of scope.

Using the AI mentor well

Ask the mentor to question your story, not to write it: "what would a tester ask about this criterion?" gets you further than "write SH-5".

criteria.title: Story
criteria.description: Who wants it, what they want, and why.

criteria.title: Acceptance criteria
criteria.description: Given / When / Then criteria a tester could check, including a book on loan.

criteria.title: Completeness
criteria.description: Enough criteria and scope lines to say what is in and what is left out.

objectives: Write SH-5 in the As a / I want / so that form
Give it at least two Given / When / Then acceptance criteria
Cover the case of a book that is already on loan

providedStories.title: Browse the shelf
providedStories.capability: to see every book in shelf order
providedStories.benefit: I can find one without asking

criteria.then: they are listed by title

criteria.when: I filter by an author in any case
criteria.then: only that author's books are listed

providedStories.title: Lend a book
providedStories.capability: to record who has borrowed a book

criteria.when: I lend it to a member
criteria.then: the book says who has it

criteria.when: I try to lend it again
criteria.then: the loan is refused

providedStories.title: Return a book
providedStories.capability: to put a returned book back
providedStories.benefit: the next member can borrow it

criteria.then: it is on the shelf again
the request is refused as not found

providedStories.title: See what is out
providedStories.capability: the shelf to say which books are on loan
providedStories.benefit: I do not walk to an empty space

criteria.then: the line ends "on loan"

phases.title: Design
phases.intro: Write down what the shelf API answers before anyone builds it: every operation, every refusal, one decision.

tasks.title: Design
tasks.brief:
Design: the shelf's contract

Fill the design in the Design room's forms: the entities and operations on the UML model tab, the endpoints and the error catalogue on the API contract tab, and one decision with its reason.

What good looks like

- The errors: which status a refusal carries (a book nobody has, a book already on loan) and the error code in its body.
- One decision, the alternative you rejected, and the reason, in a sentence with because in it.

criteria.title: Contract
criteria.description: Every operation the stories need, and every refusal with its status and error code, as a client would need them.

criteria.title: Decision
criteria.description: A decision, the alternative it beat and the reason.

criteria.title: Completeness
criteria.description: Every story the design lists is served by an operation, and every operation names its inputs and what it returns.

objectives: List every operation the API answers
Name the status and error code of every refusal
Record one decision, the alternative and the reason

stories.title: Browse the shelf
stories.line: As a member, I want to see every book in shelf order, so that I can find one without asking.

stories.title: Lend a book
stories.line: As a librarian, I want to record who has borrowed a book, so that I know where it is.

stories.title: Return a book
stories.line: As a librarian, I want to put a returned book back, so that the next member can borrow it.

phases.title: Implementation
phases.intro: The shelf runs except for four marked gaps, two in the Python API and two in the TypeScript page. Make the backlog's rules true in both.

tasks.title: Implementation
tasks.brief:
Implementation: fill the marked gaps

The shelf runs except for four marked gaps: two in the Python API (api/shelf.py: books and lend) and two in the TypeScript page (web/src/lib/shelf.ts: shelfLabel and sortForShelf). Make the backlog's rules true in both layers.

What good looks like

- books lists by title ignoring case, then id, and the author filter ignores case and surrounding spaces.
- lend refuses an unknown id, a blank borrower, and a book already on loan.
- shelfLabel and sortForShelf agree with the API about what a person reads.
- The visible tests pass before you submit; the hidden suites ask more.

Using the AI mentor well

Paste the failing test's name, not your whole file, and ask what rule it is checking. The mentor explains; it does not write the function for you.

criteria.title: Correctness (hidden tests)
criteria.description: The sealed suites, one per layer, ask the same rules many more questions.

criteria.title: Visible tests
criteria.description: The suites you can see pass, and you can run them before submitting.

criteria.title: Code quality
criteria.description: No TODO left behind, reasonable complexity, docstrings kept.

criteria.title: Process
criteria.description: You ran the tests before submitting and used the mentor in moderation.

objectives: Implement books with the author filter and shelf order (SH-1)
Implement lend and its refusals (SH-2)
Implement shelfLabel so a lent book says so (SH-4)
Implement sortForShelf so the page agrees with the API (SH-1)

phases.title: Testing
phases.intro: Write the acceptance suites that prove SH-1 to SH-4 on both sides, and catch the bugs planted in copies of the application.

tasks.title: Testing
tasks.brief:
Testing: prove the backlog

Write acceptance tests for SH-1 to SH-4 in tests/test_acceptance.py (the API) and web/src/lib/acceptance.test.ts (the page). The graders run your suites against the working application and against copies of it with bugs planted in them; a good suite passes on the first and fails on every one of the others.

What good looks like

- Every test passes against the working application.
- At least one test per acceptance criterion, asserting what a person or a client would see, not only a status code.
- Cases about the author filter, lending, returning and the "on loan" line.

Using the AI mentor well

Ask the mentor which acceptance criterion a test of yours does not yet cover.

criteria.title: Tests pass against a working application
criteria.description: A test that fails on correct code is a bug in the test.

criteria.title: Bug-detection power
criteria.description: Your suites run against broken copies of the application; a good suite fails on every one.

criteria.title: Criteria coverage
criteria.description: The author filter, lending, returning and the on-loan line each have a test.

objectives: Turn SH-1, SH-2 and SH-3 into tests over the HTTP contract
Prove the shelf line and the shelf order on the page
Make every test pass against the working application
Write assertions sharp enough to fail on every broken copy

phases.title: Deployment
phases.intro: Finish the API's image definition and the runbook, run the selfcheck, then run the drill and write down what broke.

tasks.title: Deployment
tasks.brief:
Finish api/Dockerfile so the image starts the API, and write the runbook an operator reads at 3am in the Runbook tab. Then run the selfcheck, and run the drill: a broken configuration is swapped in, and you write down what broke.

What good looks like: the Dockerfile sets a working directory, copies the application and starts api/main.py in exec form, with no TODO left. The runbook in the Runbook tab says how to check the service is healthy under Health checks and how to roll back under Rollback; its Environment and Data sections are there for anything else an operator needs. The incident is closed on the drill page with what the drill broke, the fix and one action item.

Using the AI mentor well: ask what each Dockerfile instruction changes about the image, and write the instructions yourself.

criteria.title: Config completeness
criteria.description: api/Dockerfile carries every instruction the image needs, and no TODO is left.

criteria.title: Isolated selfcheck
criteria.description: The launcher api/Dockerfile declares runs the selfcheck in the sandbox. It does not build an image.

criteria.title: Runbook quality
criteria.description: Health check, rollback and the incident, written for someone who was not there.

objectives: Complete api/Dockerfile: WORKDIR, COPY and an exec-form ENTRYPOINT
Write the runbook: health check, rollback, incident
Run the drill and record the setting that broke the deployment

phases.title: Maintenance
phases.intro: Change request CHG-1 arrives on a shelf that already works: shelve by surname. Ship it in both layers without breaking anything.

tasks.title: Maintenance
tasks.brief:
Change request CHG-1. The library has asked for the shelf to follow the order a librarian shelves in: by the author's surname, then by title, then by id. Change both layers (api/shelf.py and web/src/lib/shelf.ts) without breaking anything the shelf already did.

What good looks like: the API and the page agree on the new order. Lending, returning and the author filter behave exactly as before. The visible regression cases pass before you submit.

Record the change in the change request as you go: in the Request tab, what the change touches; in the Checks tab, the tests and the acceptance items each covers; in the Release tab, the release, its change lines and how to roll it back.

Using the AI mentor well: ask the mentor which existing behaviour your change could break, then run the regression cases to find out.

Change request CHG-1. The library has asked for the shelf to follow the order a librarian shelves in: by the author's surname, then by title, then by id. Change both layers (api/shelf.py and web/src/lib/shelf.ts) without breaking anything the shelf already did.

What good looks like: the API and the page agree on the new order. Lending, returning and the author filter behave exactly as before. The visible regression cases pass before you submit.

Record the change in the change request as you go: in the Request tab, what the change touches; in the Checks tab, the tests and the acceptance items each covers; in the Release tab, the release, its change lines and how to roll it back.

Using the AI mentor well: ask the mentor which existing behaviour your change could break, then run the regression cases to find out.
